title: The Bamboo Path

pages.text:
*Days without rain: 118. Buckets from the spring: 8.*

The bamboo forest swallowed the light. Tall, green stalks rose straight up, touching the sky, and they creaked and clicked in the small wind. It sounded like a thousand wooden sticks tapping against each other, a quiet, rhythmic clacking that seemed to have a heartbeat.

"Why do they have knots?" Tao asked. He touched a node with his finger, wincing as if it were cold. "Do they hurt when they grow?"

"No," said Hua, adjusting her red jacket. "The knot is where the leaves used to be. It is the scar of a branch that has grown away."

"And why do they make that noise?" Tao asked, tilting his head. "Are they arguing?"

"Wind pressure," Hua said, her voice precise. "The hollow stems vibrate."

Mei walked with Old Grey, the water buffalo moving with a slow, heavy grace that made the dry leaves crunch under his wide hooves. He smelled of earth and green sap. Above them, the canopy was so thick that the sun only reached the ground in thin, pale stripes.

"What if a panda lives here?" Tao asked. "What if the panda is afraid of the bamboo? Wouldn't that be terrible? He would be afraid of his own house."

Hua did not answer. She was looking at the map, her eyes scanning the lines with intense focus. Old Grey turned his wide, calm face toward Mei, and she felt a sudden, strange comfort in his patience. He was not afraid of anything. He simply walked.
pages.image: A dense bamboo forest with tall green stalks rising vertically, sunlight filtering through in thin stripes, a small girl in a blue jacket walking beside a large grey water buffalo with wide curved horns, a boy in yellow boots touching a bamboo node, soft green mist in the background.

pages.text:
Hua stopped at a fork in the path where two trails met. She held the map high, her fingers gripping the edges so tightly the paper creased. She did not look at Tao, or at Mei. She looked at the map.

"North-northwest," she read aloud. Her voice was steady, clear, and perfect, the way she sounded when she gave reports in class. "The trail bends left here. Do not take the right path. It is not a shortcut. It is a trail. There is a difference."

Tao looked at the right path. It looked shorter. It looked easier. "Why?" he asked. "Shorter is better. Faster is better. My boots are fast."

"Because," Hua said, lowering the map, "the map says so. And maps are not wrong. They are careful."

Mei watched Hua’s hands. They were shaking, just a little. The paper trembled in her grip. Mei noticed how Hua’s eyes kept darting to the trees above, to the high places, then back down to the ground. She wanted to say something, but her throat felt tight. She pressed her thumb into her palm. Old Grey made a low, rumbling sound and stepped forward, guiding them onto the left path. The sound of his bell, a single clear note, cut through the creaking bamboo. It was a sound that said: follow me.
pages.image: A fork in a dirt path through a bamboo grove, a tall girl in a red jacket holding a map with trembling hands, a boy in yellow rain boots looking at a different path, a large grey water buffalo stepping forward, dappled light on the ground.

pages.text:
They came to the dry stream bed. It was a wide road of grey stones, dry as bones, with not a drop of water in the center. But at the edge, where the stone met the earth, there was a small pool. It was no bigger than a bowl. In the center of the pool, a single tadpole swirled in a slow, black circle.

Tao dropped to his knees. His yellow boots squelched in the damp earth. "A life," he whispered. "It is alone. It is thirsty. We have to save it."

"It is a tadpole," Hua said, checking her map again. "It belongs here. The rain will come."

"The rain is not here," Tao said. He pulled a small cup from his pocket. He did not ask for permission. He scooped the tadpole and the water into the cup with the speed of a magician. "Captain," he announced. "I will take him to a wet place. Maybe a stream. Maybe a river. Somewhere with more water."

Mei looked at the empty pool. It looked sad without him. She thought of Nainai’s voice, cutting the notch in the bamboo. *Water finds a way.* Sometimes it needs help finding the way.

"Put him in the bottle," Mei said. "The big one. It has a lid."

Tao nodded solemnly. He poured the cup into the water bottle. The tadpole floated near the top, a tiny black dot against the clear water. "Captain is safe," Tao said. He tucked the bottle under his arm.
pages.image: A dry stream bed of grey stones, a small boy in yellow boots kneeling and scooping water into a cup, a single tiny black tadpole in the water, a girl in a blue jacket watching, a mossy stone in the background, soft morning light.

pages.text:
They found a mossy rock, flat and cool, and sat down to eat. Mei took out the steamed buns, white and round as small clouds. She broke one in half and offered a piece to Tao, who ate it quickly while crumbs fell on his green tiger shirt.

Hua sat apart, her knees pulled up to her chest, and held a small notebook open on her lap. Her hands were still.

"I read every map," Hua said, not looking up. "Every trail description. I checked the weather reports. I measured the distance."

"Why?" Mei asked.

"Because I want to be sure," Hua said quietly. "I don't like surprises. They are things that are not in the plan."

Mei chewed her bun slowly, the flavor sweet and plain. "I don't like being looked at," she said. The words came out soft, almost to herself, but Hua heard them.

Hua looked up, her eyes wide. "I stand at the front of the room every day. I say the words. I hold the paper. But my hands shake."

Mei really looked at her then, seeing the tightness in Hua’s shoulders and the white-knuckled grip on the notebook. They were not so different; they were two girls holding on tight to something so they wouldn't fall.

"Me too," Mei said.
pages.image: Three children sitting on a large mossy rock in a bamboo forest, a girl in a red jacket hugging her knees and holding a notebook, a girl in a blue jacket offering a white bun, a boy in yellow boots eating, soft green background, gentle and intimate mood.

pages.text:
The bamboo thinned out, the tall green stalks giving way to smaller, rougher trees until the path curved sharply to the right. The air grew heavier and cooler, and the familiar creaking of the stalks faded into a low, distant hum.

Through a gap in the branches, they saw a ridge of grey rock, jagged and high. Across it, a long thread of mist floated, white and silent, like a ribbon left behind by a passing cloud.

Hua stopped. She did not move. She took the second map from her bag, its corners worn soft from handling, and held it in her hands without opening it.

"The bridge is next," she said. Her voice was small. It was not the voice of the class monitor. It was the voice of a girl looking up at something very high. "I have read about the bridge. I know the width. I know the height."

Mei waited. She did not rush her. She stood beside her, close enough that their shoulders almost touched. The mist above seemed to hang in the air, waiting. Hua took a shaky breath. Then she took the map, and with a slow, deliberate motion, she began to unfold it.
pages.image: A view through thinning trees toward a high grey rock ridge with a band of white mist floating above, two girls standing on a dirt path, one in a red jacket holding a folded map, one in a blue jacket standing close beside her, a boy in yellow boots looking up, mysterious and quiet atmosphere.
